full_judgment:
5. After considering all the evidence and papers on record, the learned Subordinate Judge (now, Joint District Judge) 1st Court, Serajganj decreed the suit on 17-8-1994. Thereafter, the petitioner-defendant preferred Other Class Appeal No. 124 of 1994 before the Court of District Judge, Serajganj. The learned District Judge allowed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the lower Court on 1-4-1998. Against the Judgment and order of the learned District Judge, the petitioner-defendant filed the instant Civil Revision. But in the meantime the application became barred by the provision of Limitation Act because of 2825 days of delay in filing the same. 

 7. Mr Probir Neogi learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite parties Nov 3(Kha), 3(Uma), 3(Cha) and 3(Ja) submits that the impugned judgment was passed on 1-4-1998 and that the petitioner applied for certified copy of the judgment on 4-10-2004. He further submits that there is no plausible explanation whatsoever for this long delay of about 8 years for filing the instant Civil Revision. He submits that as the petitioner failed to explain each day's delay, there is no scope to condone the delay at this stage. Mr. Neogi submits that the law of limitation should be applied with all its rigour and the delay in this case should not be condoned. He next submits that the inordinate delay of 2825 days devoid of any explanation whatsoever cannot be condoned as the government has no special privilege as a litigant under the law to be indolent to the utter prejudice of citizens. Mr. Neogi relies on the decision of our Apex Court in Bangladesh is Jaheruddin 1986 BLD (AD) 180 in support of his above contention where it has been hold that: "In matters of condonation of delay Government does not enjoy any special privilege but the fact remains that due to the necessity to obtain opinions of various authorities concerned before filing an appeal, sometime may reasonably be expected to elapse which in the case of an individual does not happen. Some consideration in appropriate circumstances may, therefore, be extended to Government appearing as a litigant. In saying so, no rule is being laid down for not observing strictness of the proof of substantial and reasonable cause in making such delay. Standard of acceptance must, however, remain the same in case of both citizens and State." 

 8. I have perused the record and carefully considered the rival submissions advanced by the Advocates of the respective parties. Section 5 of the Limitation Act empowers the Court to admit an appeal or an application within the prescribed period if it is satisfied that there has been a sufficient cause for not preferring it within such period. As held by the Supreme Court of India in G Ramegowda vs Special Land Acquisition Officer AIR 1988 SC 897, the expression "sufficient cause" must receive a liberal construction so as to advance substantial justice. The power to condone delay has thus been conferred on the Court in order to enable it to do substantial justice to the parties by disposing of matters on merit. There is no denying in that the Court is required to take a broad view in the matter of condonation of limitation so as to advance the cause of justice. However, the very enactment of laws relating to limitation postulates that the parties concerned are supposed to follow their matters with due diligence. It is undoubtedly true that the decisions of the Government are collective and institutional decisions and do not share the characteristics of decisions of private individuals. Due recognition of the limitations of governmental functioning, of course, within a reasonable limit is necessary. In N Balakrishnan vs M Krishnamurthy JT 1998 (6) SC 242, the Supreme Court of India observed: 

 “It is axiomatic that condonation of delay is a matter of discretion of the Court. Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not say that such discretion can be exercised only if the delay is within a certain limit. Length of delay is no matter acceptability of the explanation is the only criterion. Sometimes delay of the shortest range may be condonable due to want of acceptable explanation whereas in certain other cases delay of very long range can be condoned as the explanation thereof is satisfactory …………” 

 In the instant case, this Court notes that the impugned judgment and decree was signed on 1-4-1998 and 13-4-1998 respectively and the petitioner applied for certified copy on 4-10-2004. There is absolutely no explanation whatsoever of the delay in between this period. Therefore, the element of negligence or inaction on the part of the authorities concerned is not ruled out at all and on the plea of liberal interpretation, the law of limitation cannot be set at naught.
